candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Find a least common denominator (LCD/LCM of denominators) and rewrite one or both fractions as equivalent fractions with that common denominator before subtracting.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three codebooks define the same operation: computing an LCD/LCM and converting to equivalent fractions with a shared denominator as a preparatory step for subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract two fractions once they share a common denominator by subtracting numerators and keeping the denominator (including like-denominator cases).
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three describe the core fraction-subtraction procedure a/b − c/b = (a−c)/b after (or without needing) common-denominator conversion.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite mixed numbers or whole numbers into an equivalent workable form for subtraction (e.g., improper fraction or separated whole+fraction, including interpreting improper mixed forms).
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A:S03 and B:S03 both focus on rewriting mixed/whole numbers (including whole-to-fraction with chosen denominator); C:S03 covers the same rewriting plus handling improper mixed forms and recombining whole+fraction, which is still the same overarching 'mixed-number handling/rewriting' concept.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Regroup/borrow between whole and fractional parts when needed and express the final answer in simplest form (reduce fractions and simplify to mixed number/integer/0 as appropriate).
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three include borrowing/regrouping when fractional subtraction would be negative and simplifying the final numeric form (reduction, 0/b→0, and final mixed/integer form). C:S04 additionally mentions rewriting a whole as a mixed number to enable borrowing, which aligns with the regrouping operation.

alignment_summary: Across A, B, and C, the skill sets align one-to-one into four shared concepts: (1) converting to a common denominator, (2) subtracting fractions with a shared denominator, (3) rewriting/handling mixed and whole numbers to make subtraction workable, and (4) regrouping/borrowing and simplifying the final result. Every expert skill_id maps cleanly to one of these four concepts, yielding 3/3 consensus for each.
